gloss: garment, clothing; deal treacherously, break faith
summary: One spelling with two meanings whose tie is not shown by the evidence. The noun בֶּגֶד is the commonest word for a garment or clothes: what Joseph left in a woman's hand, what mourners tore and the unclean washed, the holy garments of the priests, a cloth spread over the vessels of the tabernacle, and in figure the garments of salvation and vengeance, the filthy garments of iniquity, and the heavens and earth growing old like a garment. The verb בָּגַד is to break faith with one to whom one is bound: a husband with a wife, a brother with a brother, allies with their king, and Israel with Yahweh as a wife with her husband; its participle בּוֹגֵד “the treacherous” stands against the upright in Proverbs, and the nouns בֶּגֶד and בֹּגְדוֹת and the adjective בָּגוֹד are treachery and the treacherous. Arabic bijād “a striped garment” answers the noun; no cognate yet supports the verb.

words.summary: About two hundred times, almost always plural, and the general word for what is worn: beside it stand לְבוּשׁ and מְעִיל, and the particular garments (כֻּתֹּנֶת, מְעִיל, אֵפוֹד) are its kinds. It is torn in grief, washed after uncleanness, taken in pledge, and laid off and put on at the changing of the priests.

senses.definition: What a person wears; in the plural, his clothes. Given and received as goods, torn in mourning, washed for cleansing, and made of wool or linen.

evidence.note: She caught Joseph “by his garment (בְּבִגְדוֹ)”, and he left his garment in her hand and fled.
Jacob asks for “bread to eat and בֶגֶד to wear (לִלְבֹּשׁ)”: the garment is what is put on.
Isaac smelled the smell of Jacob's garments, Esau's best garments (Gen 27:15).
Silver, gold and garments given to Rebekah.
Reuben “tore his garments” when Joseph was not in the pit.
Whoever carries an unclean carcass “shall wash his garments and be unclean until evening”.
“A garment of wool or a garment of linen (פִּשְׁתִּים)”: the material it is made of.
“A garment of two kinds, שַׁעַטְנֵז, shall not come upon you.”
Tassels “on the corners of their garments”.
Each man took his garment and spread it under Jehu as he was proclaimed king.
Can a man carry fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned?
“They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing (לְבוּשִׁי) they cast lots”: בֶּגֶד in parallel with לְבוּשׁ.
The soldiers parted his garments and cast lots for his coat, that the scripture of Psa 22:19 might be fulfilled.

senses.definition: The poor man's garment, his covering by night, taken as a pledge for a debt: the law limits it and the prophets condemn its abuse.

evidence.note: “You shall not take a widow's garment in pledge (לֹא תַחֲבֹל בֶּגֶד).”
They lie down on garments taken in pledge (בְגָדִים חֲבֻלִים) beside every altar.
“Take his garment, for he has gone surety for a stranger.”
“You have stripped the naked of their garments.”
The righteous man restores the pledge, gives bread to the hungry “and covers the naked with a garment”.

senses.definition: The garments made for Aaron and his sons, “holy garments” for glory and beauty, put on to serve in the sanctuary and laid off when going out to the people, and passed from Aaron to Eleazar at his death.

evidence.note: “You shall make holy garments (בִגְדֵי־קֹדֶשׁ) for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty.”
The garments listed: breastpiece, ephod, robe, tunic, turban and sash.
Aaron and his garments are sprinkled with blood and oil and made holy.
On the day of atonement the linen tunic, undergarments, sash and turban: “they are holy garments”.
He puts off the linen garments in the tent and puts on his garments to come out.
The great priest “shall not tear his garments”.
Aaron is stripped of his garments and they are put on Eleazar his son.
The priests lay down there the garments in which they minister, “for they are holy”, and put on other garments.

senses.definition: A cloth spread over or wrapped round something: the cloths laid over the vessels of the tabernacle on the march, bedclothes, saddle cloths.

evidence.note: Over the ark they “spread a cloth (בֶּגֶד) all of blue”.
A cloth of blue, of scarlet or of purple spread over each of the holy things.
King David was old “and they covered him with garments (בַּבְּגָדִים), but he could not get warm”.
Michal covered the image in the bed with the cloth.
Dedan traded “in cloths of spreading (בְּבִגְדֵי־חֹפֶשׁ) for riding”.
Jerusalem took of her garments and made for herself high places of patches.

senses.definition: What a man is clothed with stands for what he is or what is done for him: garments of salvation, of vengeance, of beauty, filthy garments that are iniquity; and a garment that grows old and is eaten by the moth stands for what passes away.

evidence.note: Joshua stood in filthy garments; “Remove the filthy garments from him … See, I have made your iniquity pass from you, and I will clothe you with festal robes.”
“He has clothed me with garments of salvation (בִּגְדֵי־יֶשַׁע), he has wrapped me in a robe (מְעִיל) of righteousness.”
He put on “garments of vengeance (בִּגְדֵי נָקָם) for clothing” and wrapped himself in zeal as a robe.
“Their webs shall not become a garment, nor shall they cover themselves with their works.”
“All our righteousnesses are like a garment of menstruation (כְּבֶגֶד עִדִּים).”
“Put on your garments of beauty, Jerusalem, the holy city.”
The garments red from treading the winepress of the peoples.
“At every time let your garments be white.”
“They will perish, but you will stand; all of them will grow old like a garment (כַּבֶּגֶד יִבְלוּ), like clothing (כַּלְּבוּשׁ) you will change them.”
Psa 102:27 quoted of the Son: “they will all grow old like a garment.”
“They will all grow old like a garment; the moth will eat them.”
“The earth will grow old like a garment … but my salvation will be for ever.”
Man wastes away “like a garment the moth has eaten”.

evidence.locator: Gen.39.12, בִגְדוֹ → ἱματίων; Psa.22.19, בְגָדַי → ἱμάτιά; Psa.102.27, בֶּגֶד → ἱμάτιον; ἱμάτιον renders בֶּגֶד ×118

evidence.note: “They divided my garments (τὰ ἱμάτιά μου) among them”: Psa 22:19 fulfilled.
“All of them will grow old like a garment (ὡς ἱμάτιον)”: Psa 102:27.

evidence.locator: Exo.28.2, בִגְדֵי־קֹדֶשׁ → στολὴν ἁγίαν; Gen.41.42; στολή renders בֶּגֶד ×37, chiefly the priests' garments

evidence.note: “They have washed their robes (τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν) and made them white in the blood of the Lamb”: the washing of garments and white garments (Ecc 9:8) in figure.

parallels.note: “Clothing”: the fixed partner of בֶּגֶד in parallel lines.
“Robe”: garments of salvation beside a robe of righteousness, garments of vengeance beside a robe of zeal.

opposites.note: “Naked”: the righteous man covers the naked with a garment; the oppressor strips the naked of their garments.

phrases.gloss: tear one's garments (in grief or horror)

evidence.note: “Tear your heart and not your garments, and return to Yahweh your God.”

phrases.gloss: they will grow old like a garment

words.summary: About fifty times, all qal, half of them the participle בּוֹגֵד. Always faith broken where there was a bond to keep: marriage, brotherhood, alliance, the covenant. The object takes בְּ (“deal treacherously with, against”). Its tie to the noun “garment” is not shown by any evidence found: no cognate supports the verb, so the noun's Arabic cognate counts against it.

stems.gloss: deal treacherously with, break faith with, betray; (participle) the treacherous one

senses.definition: To break faith with one to whom one is bound and who trusts one: a husband with his wife, a wife with her husband, brothers and friends with one another, subjects with their king, and Israel with Yahweh.

evidence.note: “As a wife deals treacherously (בָּגְדָה) with her companion, so you have dealt treacherously with me, house of Israel.”
“The wife of your youth, with whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.”
“Let none deal treacherously with the wife of his youth … guard yourselves in your spirit and do not deal treacherously.”
The master may not sell the slave woman he took for himself “since he has dealt treacherously with her (בְּבִגְדוֹ־בָהּ)”.
“Have we not all one father? … Why do we deal treacherously a man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?”
“Even your brothers and your father's house have dealt treacherously with you … do not trust them.”
“My brothers have dealt treacherously like a wadi”: a stream that fails when it is needed.
“All her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.”
The lords of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech, whom they had made king.
“They have dealt treacherously with Yahweh, for they have borne strange children.”
“Like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt treacherously with me.”
“The house of Israel and the house of Judah have dealt very treacherously (בָּגוֹד בָּגְדוּ) with me.”
“Treacherous Judah her sister” saw Israel put away for adultery and did not fear.
“Judah has dealt treacherously … and has married the daughter of a foreign god.”
“They turned back and dealt treacherously like their fathers; they turned aside like a deceitful bow.”
“I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and from the womb you were called a transgressor.”
Saul to the people eating with the blood: “You have dealt treacherously.”
“If I had said, I will speak thus, I would have dealt treacherously with the generation of your children.”
“Wine is treacherous”: it fails the proud man who trusts it.

senses.definition: The participle as a noun, בּוֹגֵד, בֹּגְדִים: the man whose way is to break faith, set against the upright and the righteous, and in Isaiah the plunderer who breaks every agreement.

evidence.note: “The integrity of the upright (יְשָׁרִים) guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them.”
“The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are caught by their own desire.”
“The wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous rooted out of it.”
“The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the treacherous for the upright.”
“The desire of the treacherous is violence.”
Yahweh overthrows the words of the treacherous.
“Confidence in a treacherous man in a day of distress is a broken tooth and a slipping foot.”
“Those who are treacherous without cause will be ashamed.”
“I saw the treacherous and loathed them, because they did not keep your word.”
“Why do you look on the treacherous and keep silent when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he?”
“The treacherous one deals treacherously, and the destroyer (הַשּׁוֹדֵד) destroys.”
“Woe to you, destroyer … and treacherous one with whom none dealt treacherously! When you finish dealing treacherously, they will deal treacherously with you.”
“The treacherous have dealt treacherously; yes, with treachery the treacherous have dealt treacherously.”
“They are all adulterers, an assembly of treacherous men.”
“Why are all who deal treacherously with treachery at ease?”

greek.gloss: set aside, break (an agreement), deal faithlessly

evidence.locator: Jer.3.20, בָּגְדָה → ἀθετεῖ; Isa.21.2; Isa.48.8; Jer.5.11; ἀθετέω renders בָּגַד ×10

evidence.note: “Even a man's covenant, once confirmed, no one sets aside (ἀθετεῖ)”: the word's sense of breaking a covenant bond.

evidence.locator: Jer.3.11, מִבֹּגֵדָה → ἀσυνθέτου; Psa.78.57 → ἠσυνθέτησαν; Psa.119.158 → ἀσυνθετοῦντας; Psa.73.15 → ἠσυνθέτηκα

evidence.note: Among those God gave over: “without understanding, covenant-breakers (ἀσυνθέτους)”.

parallels.note: “Destroy, plunder”: the treacherous one and the destroyer side by side.
“Commit adultery”: treachery against Yahweh pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness.
“Transgress the covenant”: what the treachery is.

opposites.note: “Upright”: the integrity of the upright against the crookedness of the treacherous.

words.summary: Twice, both times as the object of the verb, “deal treacherously with treachery”. Spelled as the noun “garment”; the database files every בֶּגֶד under both keys, so its use count here is the garment's.

senses.definition: Faith broken, as the thing the treacherous do.

evidence.note: “Yes, with treachery (וּבֶגֶד) the treacherous have dealt treacherously.”
“All who deal treacherously with treachery (בֹּגְדֵי בָגֶד).”

senses.definition: Of Judah, who saw her sister Israel put away for adultery and did not return to Yahweh with all her heart.

evidence.note: “Her treacherous sister (בָּגוֹדָה אֲחוֹתָהּ) Judah saw it.”
“Her treacherous sister Judah has not returned to me with all her heart, but in falsehood.”

senses.definition: A plural of abstraction: Jerusalem's prophets are “men of treacheries”, set beside priests who profane the holy and do violence to the law.

evidence.note: “Her prophets are reckless, men of treacheries (אַנְשֵׁי בֹּגְדוֹת); her priests profane the holy.”

cognates.gloss: a striped garment of the kind called kisāʾ, worn by the Arabs of the desert; a kind of tent of soft hair
cognates.note: Arabic j answers Hebrew ג regularly. Only this noun matches: the Arabic root's other words (bajada “stay, dwell in a place”; bajdah “root, the inward truth of a matter”) share nothing with either Hebrew meaning, so the tie is the garment word alone.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 152, art. بجد, بِجَادٌ (n1771)
evidence.note: “A striped garment of the kind called كِسَآء, being one of the kinds of كَسآء worn by the Arabs of the desert … pl. بُجُدٌ. … Also a kind of tent, of [the soft hair called] وَبَر.”
Compares Arabic بِجَاد “a thick striped garment”.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh names Israel's turning from him with the word for a wife's unfaithfulness: “as a wife deals treacherously with her companion, so you have dealt treacherously with me” (Jer 3:20); Israel was put away with a bill of divorce for adultery, and “treacherous Judah” saw it and did not fear (Jer 3:8–11); “they have dealt treacherously with Yahweh, for they have borne strange children” (Hos 5:7). The treachery is a broken covenant: “like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt treacherously with me” (Hos 6:7). Malachi joins the two bonds: “have we not all one father? Has not one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously a man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?”, and Yahweh is witness between a man and “the wife of your youth, with whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant” (Mal 2:10, 14–16). Paul counts “covenant-breakers” among those God gave over (Rom 1:31). From the verses: faith kept with Yahweh and faith kept with wife and brother are one covenant obligation, because the one God made them all; to break faith with one's own is to profane the covenant with him.

Joshua the high priest stood before the angel in filthy garments; the angel said, “Remove the filthy garments from him”, and to Joshua, “See, I have made your iniquity pass from you, and I will clothe you with festal robes”, and they clothed him with garments (Zec 3:3–5). The removing of the garments is the removing of iniquity, and the clean garments are put on him by others at Yahweh's word. Isaiah says the same of the redeemed: “he has clothed me with garments of salvation, he has wrapped me in a robe of righteousness” (Isa 61:10); while of men's own deeds, “their webs shall not become a garment, nor shall they cover themselves with their works” (Isa 59:6), and “all our righteousnesses are like a polluted garment” (Isa 64:5). Those in Revelation who stand before the throne “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). From the verses: the covering that makes a man fit to stand before Yahweh is one Yahweh gives and puts on him, by taking away his iniquity; no garment a man weaves from his own works will cover him.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key בגד (b.ae.aa as BDB's root heading). Assigned: b.ae.ae בֶּגֶד garment, b.ae.aa verb, b.ae.ab בֶּגֶד treachery, b.ae.ad בָּגוֹד, b.ae.ac בֹּגְדוֹת. Shared tokens: the database files every בֶּגֶד/בִּגְדֵי under both noun keys by spelling (219 each), so b.ae.ab's use count is the garment's; treachery is only Isa 24:16 and Jer 12:1. Exo 21:8 בְּבִגְדוֹ־בָהּ, tagged qal under the noun keys, is the verb's infinitive; Gen 39:12 בְּבִגְדוֹ, filed under the verb with no stem, is the garment. Left in other entries: בַּד linen (b.ae.ak) and the verb בָּדָא (b.ae.am), filed under this root by BDB's page order, are already in bad (root בדד/בדא). Names left without name entries: בִּגְוַי Bigvai (b.ae.af), בִּגְתָן/בִּגְתָנָא Bigthan(a) (b.ae.ai, b.ae.aj) and בִּגְתָא Bigtha (b.ae.ah) are Persian names (Persian baga- “god”, the sense of the other lexicons' guess “gift of God”), not formed from the Hebrew root; if they are given entries they need a Persian source, not this root. Open questions: (1) whether the verb and the noun “garment” are one root at all: the proposed path (cover, conceal, hence act deceitfully; compare מָעַל beside מְעִיל) rests on no verse or cognate found, and the rabbinic play on בְּגָדָיו/בּוֹגְדָיו (Gen 27:27) is a later reading, not evidence; the verb therefore has no cognate and the Arabic garment word counts against it. (2) Bijād stands alone in its Arabic root; it could be a loan from Aramaic or Hebrew rather than a cognate, which would leave the noun with no independent support. Leads not followed: Ugaritic, Akkadian (none found in Oracc for bgd), Ge'ez, Old Aramaic (CAL, Hoftijzer–Jongeling) and Syriac (no ܒܓܕ in SEDRA; Payne Smith not checked). No Biblical Aramaic or Peshitta word of the root. The Septuagint renders Isa 24:16's treacherous as “those who set aside the law”; not used. No sounds recorded: ב ג ד are not merged letters.
